87

for (1) the name of the Nigerian Bar Association

and (2) the action in its entirety to be struck out.

He then proceeded to make an order not of

interlocutory injunction but of perpetual injunction

against the three learned Senior Advocates

restraining each of them from giving continued

representation to the Nigerian Bar Association or

giving representation to any other party in the suit.

The Nigerian Bar Association and the three learned

Senior Advocates being dissatisfied with the ruling

appealed successfully to the Court of Appeal. The

Court of Appeal set aside and reversed the decision

of the High Court (Candido Ademola Johnson, C.J.)

in the two applications. The Court of Appeal then

struck out (1) the name of the Nigerian Bar

Association and (2) the action on the ground that

the Nigerian Bar Association is not a juristic person

and cannot be sued eo nomine.

The Court of Appeal found nothing to justify the

order of injunction against the three learned Senior

Advocates and accordingly discharged it. It is

against this decision that the appellant has now

appealed.

The briefs filed by the appellant and the three

learned Senior Advocates are a tribute to industry

and excellence. The issues formulated and agreed

on as issues arising for determination in this appeal

are fourfold. They are:

"(1) whether the Nigerian Bar Association is a

juristic person capable of suing and being sued in

its name;

(2) whether the Chief Judge was unjustified in

barring Chief F. R. A. Williams, S.A.N., Mr. E. A.

Molajo, S.A.N. and Mr. Kehinde Sofola, S.A.N., from

appearing for the Nigerian Bar Association

consequent upon what they did and said at the

meeting of the 3rd of March, 1985 in the house of

Sir Ademola;

(3) whether the affidavit evidence sworn to on the

29th of April, 1985 by the appellant is

inadmissible;

(4) whether the Respondent waived his right to

object to the appearance of the three Senior

Advocates."

These issues have been dealt with exhaustively by

my learned brother, Agbaje, J.S.C, in the judgment

just delivered by him. His opinions on all the issues

accord with mine and I adopt them as my own.

Additionally, the importance of these issues gives

me the urge to add these further comments.

The Nigerian Bar Association celebrated its

centenary anniversary in 1986. Its existence thus

dates back to 1886. It was not a creation of statute

and has remained so without adoption by any

statute. It has of course received recognition and

mention in various statutes particularly the Legal

Practitioners Act, 1975 and the Legal Education

Act. The Legal Practitioners Act, 1975 placed the

management of the Nigerian Bar Association under

the Nigerian General Council of the Bar (see

Section 1 ). However, the Constitution of the

Nigerian Bar Association was made supreme in all

matters pertaining to the Nigerian Bar Association.

Administration of justice - Meaning of - Justice

administered by the courts is justice according to

law. When one talks of administration of justice

outside the court, the strict rules of admissibility of

evidence are relaxed and extraneous matters which

will not meet the strict rules of admissibility under

the Evidence Act are admitted and considered. In

the strict sense of the phrase known to law, no

authority other than the courts or tribunals set up

to meet the requirements of impartiality and

independence provided for by the 1979

Constitution can administer justice. When therefore

the learned Chief Judge of the Lagos High Court

observed and commented;

"The said conciliatory meeting was held while

proceedings were in court, ostensibly to aid

administration of justice by securing a settlement

among the litigants. In that role, the learned

Senior Advocates of Nigeria and elders in the

profession assumed the mantle of impartial

conciliators and the duties of an officer in aid of

justice."

He was in error.

The justice in conciliation is that of concession to

calm the atmosphere and bring peace. It has

nothing to do with determination of the rights of

the parties according to law. The misconception of

the role of conciliators in conciliatory meetings in

the search of settlement outside the walls of the

court was a fundamental error which brought about

disorientation of the learned Chief Judge in the

approach to the question of injunction before him.

It  is  not  the  law  in  Nigeria  that  any  legal

practitioner who participates in an effort to settle a

dispute already in court out of court is disqualified

and incompetent to appear for any of the parties in

the suit. He is not an arbitrator or an independent

arbiter in the sense in which a Judge is in a court

or  other  tribunal  whose  independence  and

impartiality is secured and maintained by law.

Capacity to sue and be sued; who can sue or be

sued? Any person natural or legal artificial may be

sued. This is the law in England. See Vol. 9

Halsbury's law of England 4th Ed. paragraph 1201

page 716 . It is also the law in Nigeria. See section

6(6)(b) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic,

1979 .

Who is a natural person? It is a human person who

has life and blood in him or her whether a citizen of

one State or another given protection by law and

endowed with human qualities.

Who is an artificial or legal person? Usually, it is a

corporation aggregate or sole. It can be created by

law, e.g. University of Ibadan Act, 1962, University

of Lagos Act, 1967 or incorporated under the law,

e.g. companies under the Companies Act, 1968.

Corporation aggregate and corporation sole have

been given adequate definitions in Halsbury's Laws

of England. Juridical personality is not equivalent to

a  juristic  personality.  Juridical  personality  is

acquired when the law accepts and recognizes the

existence  of  unincorporated  associations.  The

capacity of suing and being sued is not thereby

given by the mere recognition and acceptance of its

existence. Thus, the acceptance and recognition by

(a) The Legal Practitioners' Act, 1975 ( Sections 1 ,

3 , 7 , 9 , 11 , 14 , 22 and 23 thereof);

(b) Legal Education (Consolidation etc.) Act, 1976

as amended by the Legal Education Consolidation

etc. Act, 1977 ( Sections 19  and  27  thereof);

(c) The Interpretation Act, 1964 ( Section 2(1)

thereof)

(d)  Item 48 of the Exclusive Legislative List of the

Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria,

1979  cannot be construed as the conferment on the

Nigerian Bar Association of the capacity to sue.

Only the law of the land can confer that attribute or

capacity and in most statute the capacity to sue

and be sued of the authority or body they create is

expressed. Where not expressed, the implication will

be obvious from the expressed provisions of the

statute especially where a power given to it may be

exercised to the detriment of others.

See Thomas v. Local Government Service Board

(1965) 1 All N.L.R. 168. See Forest City MFG. ETAL .

v. Garment Workers' Union . 233 Missouris Report

1975 (A decision of St. Louis Court of Appeal). Taff

Vale Railway Co. v. Amalgamated Society of

Railway Servants (1901) A.C. 426; Amalgamated

Society of Carpenters, Cabinet Makers & Joiners v.

Braithwaite , (1922) 2 A.C. 440. Bonsor v.

Musicians' Union (1954) Ch. 479 (1956) A.C. 104;

Willis v. Association of Universities of the British

Commonwealth (1965) 1 Q.B. 140 Knight and

Searle v. Dove (1964) 2 Q.B. 631; Solicitor

General Western Nigeria v. Adedoyin (1973)

U.I.L.R.143.

"The legal characteristics of a registered trade

union differentiate it from other voluntary

associations and may entitle it to be called a legal

entity, while at the same time remaining

an unincorporated association of individuals." per

Lord Keith of Avonholm in Bonsor v. Musicians'

Union (supra).

The Constitution of the Nigerian Bar Association is

not a statutory instrument. It is not a subsidiary

legislation to the Legal Practitioners Act. It is a

pure  and  simple  private  document  which  the

members of the Nigerian Bar Association were

entitled to draw up in exercise of their right to

provide  a  constitution  for  the  Association  to

regulate its affairs. It was accorded its due superior

position by the Legal Practitioners Act, 1975 in the

conduct  of  the  affairs  of  the  Nigerian  Bar

Association by the General Council of the Bar. This

does not make the Nigerian Bar Association a

juristic person. It only gives the body recognition as

a legal entity made up of legal practitioners. The

fact  that  the  legislature  has  in  the  Legal

Practitioners Act, 1975 and the Legal Education

(Consolidation etc.) Act, 1976 given the Nigerian

Bar Association representation on the Body of

Benchers and the Council of Legal Education is no

indication   that   legislature   constituted   the

Association a suable entity.

It is significant to know that the Nigerian Bar

Association can only own property, or interest in

land by Trustees appointed under section 13 of its

Constitution Exhibit F. The name 'Nigerian Bar

Association' is not a registered name under any

statute although it is recognized and accepted as

the name of the body by various statutes.

The Nigerian Bar Association loses nothing by being

declared a non juristic person. It can always sue

and be sued in a representative capacity. The

representative action is always available to it and

to all persons wronged by it. The various State High

Court Civil Procedure Rules make provisions for

representative actions.

The decision of the Court of Appeal on the first

issue is therefore in accordance with and justified

by the law.

Turning to the second issue as I said earlier, the

learned Chief Judge was fundamentally in error in

holding that Chief F. R. A. Williams, S.A.N., Mr. E.

A. Molajo, S.A.N. and Mr. Kehinde Sofola, S.A.N.,

were constituted into independent and impartial

arbiters disqualified from giving legal

representation to any of the parties because they

participated in the unsuccessful move to settle the

dispute between the parties out of court after the

originating summons was filed. They would have

preferred a domestic settlement rather than an

action in court.

Was their appearance improper, unprofessional,

dishonorable and dishonest? This question arises

because allegations contained therein constituted

the main ground for the application for the order of

injunction. I will regard the allegation as complaint

of a breach of professional conduct in the legal

profession Beyond the mere allegation, were there

facts adduced constituting and proving an infamous

conduct and a breach of professional conduct?

The relevant rules of professional conduct in the

legal profession that requires examination in the

list of the complaints are Rules 4(a) , (b) , (c) , (d) ,

(e) and (f) ; 10(10) and (b) ; 14(a) , (b) and (c) ; 21 ,

22 , 24 and 26 .

Having examined the facts in the light of the above

rules, I agree with my learned brother. Agbaje,

J.S.C, and the Court of Appeal that it has not been

established that any of the three learned Senior

Advocates has breached any of the said Rules.

The facts containing admissions recorded from the

peace meeting cannot in law be admitted in the

court proceedings and I agree with my learned

brother that the affidavit evidence containing those

admissions produced by the appellant is

inadmissible.

The right of the plaintiff/appellant to complain of a

breach of Rules of Professional Conduct is a right to

promote the course of justice and as the promotion

of the course of justice is an ever present duty on

all, especially officers of the court as the appellant

is, that right can not be waived.

However, as the appellant has failed to establish

any breach, the second issue must be resolved

against him. The appeal therefore fails and is

hereby dismissed with N500.00 costs to each set of

respondents.

The decision of the Court of Appeal is hereby

affirmed.

ADOLPHUS GODWIN KARIBI-WHYTE, J.S.C. : I have

read the judgment of my learned brother, Agbaje, J.S.C.

in this appeal. I have been persuaded by the force of the

arguments and the conclusions that flow from them

and I agree with both. I also will dismiss this

appeal. I only wish to make some contribution to

the subject-matter of this appeal, which though not

entirely novel, are of the most important

significance and relevance in our jurisprudence.

The background to the litigation and the judicial

history of this appeal which have been stated with

meticulous care and clarity in my learned brother,

Agbaje, J.S.C.'s judgment are adopted in their

entirety. With the exception of the question for

determination concerning the justification for an

order for injunction, included by the 1st-4th

Respondents both the Appellant, and the 1st - 4th

Respondents expressing it fairly differently, agree

that the issues for determination are whether

1. That the N.B.A. is a juristic person capable of

being sued in its name.

2. The Chief Judge was unjustified in barring the

2nd-4th Respondent from appearing for the N.B.A.

consequent upon what they did and said at the

meeting of the 3rd March, 1985 in the house of Sir

Ademola.

3. The affidavit evidence sworn to on the 29th of

April, 1985 by the Appellant is inadmissible.

4. The Respondent waived his right to object to the

appearance of the three Senior Advocates.

I will therefore adopt the above formulation of the

questions for determination in this judgment.

This judgment is concerned only with the first

question, the determination of which is crucial to all

the declarations sought. For this purpose I shall

confine myself to grounds 1 and 2 of the six

grounds of appeal filed by the appellant.

The grounds of appeal together with the particulars

of error complained of are as follows -

"1. The learned Justices of the Court of Appeal

erred in law in striking out the Nigerian Bar

Association on the ground that it is not a juristic

person capable of being sued

WHEN:

(1) Having regard to several statutory and

constitutional provisions conferring rights and

imposing duties and functions on the Nigerian Bar

Association, it must be taken as a juristic person or

a legal personality capable of being sued.

(2) There is nothing in Thomas v. Local

Government Service Board (1965) 1 All N.L.R. 168

heavily relied upon by the Court of Appeal

precluding that court from considering statutory

provisions relating to the Nigerian Bar Association

in determining whether or not it is a juristic person

capable of being sued.

The Court of Appeal misdirected itself in law in the

lead judgment by saying:

". . . I cannot agree with Chief Fawehinmi that the

Constitution of the Association is a statutory or

subsidiary instrument within the meaning of the

law. . ."

Particulars of Misdirection

(1) Section 1 of the Legal Practitioners Act, 1962

(replaced by Section 1 of the Legal Practitioners

Act, 1975 ) must be taken as empowering the

Nigerian Bar Association to make its own

Constitution.

(2) The Constitution so made by the Nigerian Bar

Association ought to be taken as a Subsidiary

Instrument by virtue of the provisions of the

Interpretation Act of 1964.

(3) Consequently the Constitution of the Nigerian

Bar Association is a Subsidiary Instrument i.e. a

Law.

I have copied the particulars of error relied upon by

the appellant because of their assumed relevance

to the grounds of appeal and propositions, of law

contended for Chief Gani Fawehinmi for himself,

and all counsel to the parties in this case, namely,

Chief Gani Fawehinmi for himself, and all counsel to

the parties in this case, namely, Chief F. R. A. Williams

S.A.N., for the 1st-4th Respondents and Kehinde

Sofola, S.A.N., for the 4th Respondent filed briefs

of argument. Mr. M. Adio, Director, Civil Litigation,

Federal Ministry of Justice, appeared for the

5th Respondent. They all adopted their briefs of

argument and relied on them in their argument before

us.

The issue for determination in grounds 1 & 2 of the

grounds of appeal filed in the first issue for

determination agreed by all the parties. This is

whether the Nigerian Bar Association is a juristic

person capable of being sued in its own name, i.e.

eo nomine? Chief Gani Fawehinmi contended that it

is. He relied on several decided cases in this

country, in England, Canada and Australia, and the

practice in the International Court of Justice in

support of the contention. His main thesis is that

the recognition accorded by legislation to the

existence in fact as an association of persons of the

Nigeria Bar Association per se, and the fact that it

has a constitution which governs its affairs, and the

legal provisions enabling the association to

nominate its members into bodies established by

law, were sufficient to raise the implication that the

Association is itself not only regarded but is a

creature of the law with all the attributes of legal

personality by artificial persons created by law.

The contrary contention by the Respondents is that

the Nigerian Bar Association is an Association of

persons recognized by law. To that extent, it is a

persona juridica. It is not an association of persons

distinct from the persons who constitute it to make

it a juristic person; i.e. a legal person subject of

rights and duties in law. It has no separate

existence. It is therefore not a juristic person

capable of being sued and to sue eo nomine.

All counsel in their arguments relied on the same

decided cases, but appellants and Respondents

adopting different interpretations as to what the

cases should be understood as having decided. It is

important to point out that there is some measure

of agreement on the general conclusion that the

Nigerian Bar Association is undeniably an

unincorporated association. This was the argument

of Chief Fawehinmi in the alternative. The

divergence of views arose where appellant took the

view that the Nigerian Bar Association should be

treated as a legal person because the law having

recognized is as an association of persons, imposed

certain duties on it.

The well  settled judicial  view in this country

appears to  me  consistent  in  holding that  an

association of persons without incorporation cannot

be regarded as a legal person for the purposes of

actions in court. Forty-eight years ago in   Amodu

Rufai Shitta and Ors. v. Momodu Ligali and Ors .

(1941) 16 N.L.R. 23, twelve persons regarding

themselves in the writ as the "Executive of the

Central Mosque", purported to sue in that capacity.

It was held that the Committee was nothing more

than a collection of individuals and had no capacity

to sue. Thus the "Executive of the Central Mosque"

was held not to be a juristic person . See also

Martins v. Federal Administrator-General (1963) L.

L. R. 65; Agbonmagbe Bank v. G. B. Ollivant Ltd.

(1961) All N.L.R. 116; Ekpere v. Aforije (1972) 3

S.C. 113. The proposition that an action is only

maintainable by a legal person was clearly brought

out in the recent decision of this Court in Nurses

Association v. Attorney-General (1981) 11-12 SC.

Thus the onus is on the party claiming the status of

a juristic person derived from incorporation or not

to establish it. In this Court, in Apostolic Church,

Ilesha, v. A.G. (Mid West) (1972) 4 SC. 150 it was

held that the corporate status of a body is

established by the production of its certificate of

incorporation.

Chief Gani Fawehinmi in his effort to discharge this

onus had relied in his submission on the

Constitution of the Nigerian Bar Association,

Statutes, and the rights and privileges conferred by

Statutes and the Constitution of the Federal

Republic of Nigeria, 1979 to contend that the

Nigerian Bar Association is a juristic person capable

of suing and of being sued eo nomine.

Both Chief Williams, S.A.N., and Kehinde Sofola,

S.A.N., have submitted that none of the statutes

relied upon by Chief Fawehinmi support his

contention. Accordingly, it was submitted the Court

of Appeal was right in holding that the Nigerian Bar

Association is not recognized in law "for purposes of

suing or being sued in its own name," although it is

recognized "as a separate entity for a variety of

purposes." Mr. Adio for the 5th Respondent adopted

their submissions.

It is important to discuss the general concept of the

creation of legal personality in our law before

examining the claim by Chief Fawehinmi that the

right to sue and be sued had been vested in the

Nigerian Bar Association on implication from the

various statutory provisions he relied upon. Before

embarking on this analysis it is pertinent to

observe that Respondents are not disputing the fact

that the N.B.A. is an association of persons

recognised in law. The point of difference is

whether such recognition amounts to vesting on

the Association the legal attributes of incorporation,

i.e. the right to sue and be sued in its own name.

It is convenient to start with the provisions of

Section 37 of the Constitution 1979 which provides:

"Every person shall be entitled to assemble freely

and associate with other persons, and in particular

he may form or belong to any association for the

protection of his interests;......."

Thus, the right to form any association for the

protection of the interests of the members is

guaranteed under this provision of the Constitution

1979 and is an entrenched right. However, such

association of persons, though recognised by the

Constitution does not ipso facto vest in the

Association the attributes of incorporation which

alone confers legal personality. It is for this reason

that the power to incorporate such associations has

been provided under Items 31 and 48 of the

Schedule 2 Part 1 of the Constitution 1979. Items

31 and 48 enable the National Assembly, and now

the Armed Forces Ruling Council, to make laws with

respect to

"31. Incorporation, regulation and winding up of

bodies corporate, other than co-operative societies,

local government councils, and bodies corporate

established directly by any Law enacted by a House

of Assembly of a State.

"48. Professional occupations as may be designated

by the National Assembly."

Thus an association of persons recognised by

Section 37 is a lawful association simpliciter. It is a

recognition of the reality that the group of persons

who have formed an association has an existence in

fact. In strict legal theory, only human beings are

subject of rights and duties. And even in the case of

human beings, the law differentiates between

persons capable of exercising an independent will of

their own and those who due to infancy or other

disability are incapable. Thus there are human

beings with rights but without correlative duties. A

natural person is a legal person not because he is a

human being, but because rights and duties are

inherent from the status, and are ascribed to him.

A natural person is the legal subject or substance of

which rights and duties are attributes. This is the

status of every full citizen.

Our law seems to me to endorse the proposition

that no association of any kind could be formed

without being authorised by the State. Groups of

persons behave as individuals and exercise the

collective responsibilities, rights and duties of the

group. In ordinary language, this exercise of

collective rights and duties is personified in the

group. Hence we personify the family, the town or

indeed the clan without the group being recognised

as a distinct legal entity separate from its

members. The grant of legal personality of the kind

possessed by full citizens without legal disability is

only capable of being donated by the state. In the

case of Sutton's Hospital , Coke referred to

corporations as, "invisible, immortal, vesting only

in the intendment of the law." - See 10 Co. Rep.

Rep. 1(a) 32. Again in Dartmouth College v.

Woodward 4 Wheat 518 at p. 636, Marshall, C.J in

1819 defined a corporation as "an artificial being

invisible, intangible, and existing, only in

contemplation of the law." Hence legal or juristic

personality is not attained until the law recognises

over and above the associated individuals, a single

entity which represents them, but is not identical

with them.

Chief Fawehinmi relies on the recognition of the

existence of the Nigerian Bar Association by the

provisions of the Legal Practitioners Act, 1975

Sections 1(1) , 1(2) , 3(3)(9) , 3(3)(f) , 9(2)(c) , S. 23

Legal Education (Consolidation, etc.) Act 1976,

s.2(1) , Legal Education (Consolidation, etc.) Act

1977, S.2(1) ; I shall hereafter refer to the National

Bar Association as the Association.

These legislations relate to the creation of the body

known as the General Council of the Bar, which is

charged with the Management of the affairs of the

Nigerian Bar Association, S.1(1) , and also provides

for members of the "Association" to be members of

the General Council of the Bar, otherwise known as

the Bar Council- S.1(2) to be elected by members of

the Association in the manner provided by the

Constitution of the Association and to hold office as

provided by the Constitution of the "Association."

By S.3(3)(g) , the Association is to nominate its

members to the Body of Benchers. The President of

the "Association" is made a member of the Body of

Benchers by S.3(1)(f) . Again, the "Association" is

entitled to nominate members to the Legal

Practitioners Disciplinary Committee - S.9(2)(c) . By

s.2(1) of the Legal Education (Consolidation, etc.)

Act 1976 as amended by an Act of 1977 of the

same name, the "Association" is entitled to appoint

its members to the Legal Education Council, and to

have its President as a member.

It is important to observe that in none of the

legislations referred to is the Nigerian Bar

Association eo nomine named as a member of the

other bodies created by the statutes. The person

required to be members are either a prescribed

number of the members or the President of the

Association. It seems to me clear that the

legislature providing for the exercise of the duties

recognise the Association as unincorporated, and

accordingly have expressly provided for the manner

in which the obligation will be discharged. The

recognition by the legislations that the

"Association" has a Constitution which governs its

relationship with its members, and of the members

inter se is not inconsistent with the concept of an

unincorporated association recognised by the

Constitution of the country and does not imply a

recognition that the Association is thereby entitled

to enjoy the attributes of incorporation without

incorporation.

Chief Fawehinmi also relied on the membership of

the "Association", the fact that the subscription

payable annually is regulated by the legal

Practitioners Act, 1975 and that a specific

percentage of the fees so paid is appropriated for

the Association as part of his contention that the

Association is a statutory body, a juristic person

capable of suing and being sued.

I agree with the submissions of counsel to the

Respondents and have found it fairly difficult to

understand the contention that because the"

Association" is recognised as a professional

association of lawyers, that membership of the

Association is automatic on being a legal

practitioner registered under the Act, and that part

of the fees paid by legal practitioners is

appropriated for the use of the Association, it is a

creation of statute. The misconception in the

argument is one of confusing a body which is

recognised as a personification of the members as a

separate entity in fact, and capable of acting on its

own behalf through certain persons who constitute

and are inextricably part of the body, and that of

recognition of the "Association" as a distinct legal

entity capable of acting on its own behalf, and

owning property without recourse to members of

the Association. This was the conclusion the Court

of Appeal drew, and correctly in my opinion when it

said, referring to the statutes relied upon by Chief

Fawehinmi,

"All the several statutes which relate to the

Association show that the law recognises the

Association as being in existence.

Chief Fawehinmi was therefore right when he

submitted that in view of those numerous statutes

which have referred to the Association we cannot

but come to the conclusion that it exists as a

separate entity distinct from its members. But in

my judgment, it is misconception to say that

because it is a separate legal entity, it is

necessarily a separate legal entity, a juristic person

whereby it can sue and be sued eo nomine. To put

it in another way, it is a separate entity de facto

but not a separate, legal entity, de jure, for

purposes of prosecuting a suit in its own name."

Chief Gani Fawehinmi has submitted that the

"Association" by virtue of the Statutes referred to

especially Sections 1 (1) of the Legal Practitioners

Act 1975 which recognised the Constitution of the

Association and Section 23 which corrected the

name of the Association from the Nigerian Bar

Association to the Nigeria Bar Association suggests

that the Association is a creation of the statute.

It is difficult to construe, even if one wants to do so

in bad faith, any of the statutes relied upon as

having created the Nigerian Bar Association. By no

stretch of the imagination can the words used lead

to such a construction. This is because Section 1(1)

of the Legal Practitioners Act 1975 which

established the General Council of the bar and

provides that the body shall be charged with the

Management of the 'Nigeria' Bar Association, went

on in Section 3 to establish the Body of Benchers

and to provide in Section 3(2) that

"The Body of Benchers shall be a body corporate

with perpetual succession and common seal."

Similarly, Section 5(3) established the Legal

Practitioners' Privileges Committee of the General

Council of the Bar, and Section 9(1) established the

legal Practitioners Disciplinary Committee; and

Section 11(1) The Appeal Committee of the Body of

Benchers charged with the duty of hearing appeals

from the Disciplinary Committee. There are other

Committees of the General Council of the Bar

established under the Legal Practitioners Act 1975

and charged with various statutory duties. These

are creations of the statute and are accordingly

vested with the attributes of legal persons.

By the application of the interpretation rule of

expression unions est exclusio alterius, the

Nigerian Bar Association cannot be construed

among the express creations of the bodies to the

Legal Practitioners Act, 1975 and is therefore not

one of the creations of the statute as the

Committees mentioned above. Any provisions of

the statutes referred to or any other legislation

does clearly not support Chief Fawehinmi's

submission that the Nigerian Bar Association is a

statutory body created by statute. Chief Fawehinmi

submitted in his brief argument and before us

statutes, Legal Practitioners Act and the

Constitution of the Nigerian Bar Association,

regulate that membership of the Association. The

basis for this submission is because Article 4 of the

Constitution as the Association provides that "Every

person duly enrolled by virtue of the Legal

Practitioners Act shall be a member of the

Association....." I do not think this article can be

construed as having any statutory effect or to have

converted a non-statutory provision of the

Constitution of the Association, (the Constitution

not being the creation of statute) into a statutory

provision. Membership of the Association on being a

legal practitioner is automatic, but this is merely a

pre-condition of Membership of the Association as

provided by Article 4 of the Constitution of the

Association, which is not a statutory provision.

What regulates Membership of the Association is

the provision of its constitution and not the

provision of the Legal Practitioners Act, 1975. The

fact that reference is made to Membership of the

Association in a legislation did not alter the true

legal situation. The recognition accorded the

Association and its Constitution did not give

statutory effect to the Constitution of the

Association or make the Association a Statutory

Body. Our Constitution in Item 48 of the second

schedule provides that incorporation of professional

bodies can only be attained through a legislation of

the National Assembly. This has not been done in

this case.

It is relevant to point out and it seems to me that

the Association was quite conscious of its status as

an unincorporated Association, and legal defect as a

body hence it took precaution in Article 13 of its

Constitution to empower its National Executive to

provide for the appointment of trustees who shall

inter alia, deal with the properties of the

Association as directed to apply for Registration

under the Land Perpetual Succession Act. Cap.98

Laws of Nigeria. By Section 2(3) of this Act the

Trustees when registered "shall thereupon become

a body corporate by the name described in the

certificate and shall have perpetual succession and

a common seal, and power to the conditions and

directions contained in the certificate to hold, and

acquire, and by instruments under such common

seal to convey, assign and demise, any land or

interest therein now or hereafter belonging to, or

held for the benefit of such community, body or

association of persons, in such and the like manner,

and subject to such restrictions, and provisions, as

such trustees or trustee might, without such

incorporation, hold or acquire, conveyor assign, or

demise the same for the purposes of such

community, body or association of persons."

By a combined reading of Sections 3 and 8 of this

law, the Trustees will operate in their registered

name as an incorporated body on behalf of the

Association. Thus the Association having provided

for its trustees to be registered for the purposes

stated above were conscious of its legal status as

an unincorporated Association.

In Williams v. Sanusi (1961) 1 All N.L.R. 334, the

Federal Supreme Court held that where a body is

registered under the Land (Perpetual Succession)

Act, the trustees can sue or be sued under the

name provided in the Certificate of incorporation. It

is properly arguable that such actions will be

limited to those matters covered by that law and in

respect of which the Trustees have the authority.

Even if this was conceded, the Association has no

capacity eo nomine to bring actions or be sued.

Registration was devised to obviate such problem.

Where the Nigerian Bar Association has the status

of a legal person, registration under the Lands

(Perpetual Succession) Act would have been

unnecessary.

It may be conceded that no particular form of words

are required for the purpose of creating a

corporation, where the intention to incorporate is

evident from the words used - See Tone River

Conservators v. Ash 10 B & c. 349. I now turn to

the decided cases cited and relied upon by Chief

Fawehinmi as authority for his proposition that the

Association is a creation of Statute, which can sue

and be sued in its own name. There are the cases

of Thomas v. Local Government Service Board

(1965) 1 All N .L.R. 168; Kpebimoh v. Board of

Governors, Western Ijaw Teachers' Training College

(1966) 1 N .M.L.R. 130; Solicitor-General, Western

Nigeria v. Adedoyin , CA W/83/69 of 30th August,

1971; Adedeji v. Police Service Commission (1968)

N. M. L. R. 102.

There are also the decisions founded on the English

Trade Union Acts 1871 and 1876, and now Trade

Unions and Labour Relations Act 1974 such as

Bonsor v. Musicians Union (1956) A.C. 104; Vine v.

National Dock Labour Board (1957) A.C. 488; Taft

Vale Railway v. Amalgamated Society of Railway

Servants (1901) A.C. 426; Willis v. Association of

Universities of the British Commonwealth (1964) 2

All E.R. 39. The Canadian case of Bass v.

Pharmaceutical Association of British Columbia

(1965) 51 D.L.R. (2D.) 552; the Australian case of

Clyne v. The New South Wales Bar Association

(1960) 104 C.L.R. 186.

I shall begin with the Australian case of Clyne v.

New South Wales Bar Association (supra). The New

South Wales Bar Association, a voluntary

association of barristers incorporated in 1936, with

powers to exercise supervision over the conduct of

members of the Bar, and to lay down rules and

decide questions of professional conduct and

etiquette, sought an order of the full court of New

South Wales that the name of the appellant be

struck off the roll of barristers of the State of New

South Wales on the ground that he has been found

guilty of such grave professional misconduct as

shown him not to be a fit and proper person to

practice as a barrister. The issue of its capacity to

sue did not arise as it was well known to be an

incorporated body. This case does not therefore

support the appellant. Again, in Bass v.

Pharmaceutical Association of British Columbia

(supra) the Pharmaceutical Association of British

Columbia was registered under the Pharmacy Act of

British Columbia, 1960. The Council of the

Association was empowered to make Bye-Laws and

Regulations. Bass, a member of the Association

brought an action challenging the validity of the

Bye-law and seeking a declaration that it was ultra

vies the Act. The question whether the

Pharmaceutical Association was a legal person

capable of suing and being sued did not arise in the

circumstance. The Association was established

under the Pharmacy Act of British Columbia, 1960.

As Kehinde Sofola, S.A.N., pointed out, and is clear

from the report of the case, "the apparent objects

of the Pharmacy Act are to establish the Defendant

Association as a body politic and corporate . . . etc."

Obviously, therefore the Pharmaceutical

Association of British Columbia was established

under the Pharmacy Act of British Columbia and

therefore a statutory body.

The English cases of Taff Vale Railway v.

Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants (Supra);

Bonsor v. Musicians Union (1956) A. C. 104; Vine

v. National Dock Labour Board (supra) based on the

interpretation of the Trade Union Acts are quite

different. A careful analysis of the Trade Union Acts

1871 and 1876 discloses no provision enabling

incorporation of Trade Unions. Indeed Registration

of Trade Unions in certain statutes including

Companies Acts shall be void - S.5 . But the Unions

when registered can make purchases or leases in

the names of trustees. A Trade Union, which is not

registered under the Acts, does not enjoy any of

the privileges of registration. By Section 9 a

registered Trade Union is entitled to sue and can be

sued in the names of its trustees or authorised

officers. However, the Act of 1871 did not

incorporate Trade Unions even when registered

under the Act with a name. The present Trade

Unions and Labour Relations Act 1974, does not

treat a Trade Union as a Corporate body, but

enables them in S.2(1)(c) to sue and be sued in

their registered names, and S.3(1)(b) also enables

unincorporated employers association to sue and be

sued in its own name in all actions. The decided

cases concede that Trade Unions are "when

registered, quasi-corporations, resembling much

more closely railway companies incorporated by

statute than voluntary associations of individuals

merely bound together by contract agreement,

express or implied" - See Atkinson, L.J. in

Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants v.

Osborne (1910) A.C. 87. The provisions of the

Trade Union Acts clearly and necessarily imply the

power to sue or being sued in the Society's name is

clearly and necessarily implied by the provisions

of the Trade Union Acts.

Willis v. Association of Universities of British

Commonwealth (supra), though not a trade union

case was decided on the principle, that the

Association of Universities of British Commonwealth

is a limited company and that the Universities

Central Council on Admissions was not a separate

and independent body, except from the financial

stand point where it is treated separately. It is not

a body corporate. But the Court of Appeal held it

could be so treated under S.23(2) of the Landlord

and Tenant Act 1954 . This is on the interpretation

of "activity" within S.23(2) . This is not a good

illustration of the ascription of legal personality

because it is limited to the special purposes of the

Act.

In each of the cases of Thomas v. Local

Government Service Board (supra), Kpebimoh v.

Board of Governors Western Ijaw Teachers'

Training College (supra); Solicitor General,

Western Nigeria v. Adedoyin (supra), the bodies in

the first two cases were created by statutes and the

last, a constitutional office, where vested were

statutory functions. The Local Government Service

Board in Thomas v. Local Government Service

Board (supra) was created by Section 93 of the

Local Government Law . Section 98 conferred on its

members immunity from suits for official conduct,

and there is no provision expressly enabling it to

sue or be sued, or to own property. However,

Section 97 which provides for a claim for privilege

for the Records of the Board and Section 98 already

referred to imply that the Legislature is making

these provisions envisaged that the Board can sue

and can be sued. The immunity conferred on the

members for official conduct is not an immunity

which the Board eo nomine can claim. The

considerations taken into account why the

Legislature implied legal personality in the Board

were the nature of the statutory functions relating

to the office of the Board which might result in

injustice unless it could be made a Defendant in

any proceedings challenging the exercise of such

duties. The Supreme Court however pointed out

that the Customary Laws by implication from

Section 5 of the Customary Courts Law as amended

by the Customary Courts (Amendment) Law, 1959

vests in the Board the power to appoint, dismiss

and exercise disciplinary control, including

suspension of Presidents or Vice Presidents of

Customary Courts. It is the appointing authority for

all members of a Customary Court.

No similar statutory duties have been vested in the

Nigerian Bar Association by any statute to be

exercised by the Association. The obligation of

nominating or electing its members into bodies

established by law, or the automatic membership of

its President in such bodies are not such statutory

duties.

Like Thomas v. Local Government Service Board

(supra) discussed, Kpebimoh's case involved the

Board of Governors, Western Ijaw Teachers'

Training College, a body established under Section

53 of the Education Law, Cap.34 . The instrument of

Management listed various functions which the

Board, though not incorporated, but established by

law is empowered to discharge. It is therefore

reasonable to imply that the Board in the discharge

of these functions will exercise the rights of a legal

person and will if the nature of the duty discharged

so involved, be suable in the courts, i.e. possess

juristic personality. The General Council of the Bar,

the 5th Respondent in this appeal which is the body

established under Section 1(1) of the Legal

Practitioners Act 1975 is the body charged with the

general management of the affairs of the

Association, the first Respondent. This is

comparable to the position of the Association of

Universities of the British Commonwealth in

relation to its National Council on Admissions in

Willis v. Association of Universities of the British

Commonwealth (supra).

The decision of the High Court of Australia in the

case of Chaff and Hay Acquisition Committee & Ors.

v. J. A. Hemphill & Sons Proprietary Ltd. (1946-47)

74 C.L.R. 375 is a valid illustration of ascription of

legal personality by implication. The Chaff and Hay

Committee was a statutory body created under the

Chaff and Hay (Acquisition) Act 1944 (S.A.). The

Committee of four established by S.3 was

authorised inter alia, to acquire within and without

the state certain property, which on acquisition, it

held in its collective name, Sections 4 , 5(1) , 8 . It was

also empowered to dispose of property and to sue

in its collective name Section 14(1) . The Act

contained no express words of incorporation and

the committee had no common seal. It was

contended that the Committee was not a legal

entity, having not been incorporated. The appellant

conceded among other submissions that the

committee possessed all the characteristics of a

corporation with the exception of the words of

incorporation and the attributes of a perpetual

succession and common seal. These it was argued

were vital and fatal.

The words of the enabling provisions clearly showed

that the property and rights acquired and liabilities

incurred by the Committee were those of the

Committee and not of the members. Accordingly, it

was held that the Committee is a legal entity in

South Australia distinct from the persons

composing it from time to time, with the property,

rights and liabilities belonging to it and not to those

persons.

Legal personality can only be conferred by statute.

It may be conferred for a limited purpose as was

done in respect of the Minister of Health in

England, to acquire and hold land - Gilleghan v.

Minister of Health (1932) 1 K.B. 86. This seems to

me a notion of qualified personality which Fullagar,

J. in Williams v. Hursey (1960) 103 C.L.R. 30 at p.

52 regards as unintelligible. I do not share the

opinion. It is clearly not inconsistent with the

possession of legal personality that the capacity of

the persona should be limited.

The most fundamental of the differences between a

corporation and an unincorporated association are

that the corporation has "perpetual succession," it

maintains its identity and its personality,

notwithstanding changes in its membership; its

property does not belong to its members. But the

property of an unincorporated association does

belong to its members from time to time, and that

property may be owned by entirely different

persons at the date when the cause of action arose,

at the date when the action is commenced, and at

the date when the judgment is pronounced. The

cases I have considered are sufficient for the

purposes of this judgment. I intend no disrespect

for not considering the other cases to which we

were referred.

It seems to me that the Association cannot by

implication from the exercise of any functions

imposed on it by statute enjoy the attributes of

juristic personality acquired only upon

incorporation. The Court of Appeal was accordingly

right when it held as follows:

"The true position appears to me to be that the law

recognises an association such as the first appellant

as a separate entity for a variety of purposes but

not for the purposes of suing or being sued in its

own name."

I agree with this conclusion as

accurately representing the correct legal position.

Since the declaration sought is against the

Association, against whom an action cannot be

brought in its own name, the Court of Appeal came

to the correct decision by striking out its name from

the summons. Authority for the principle which are

well settled can be found in Agbonmagbe Bank Ltd.

v. General Manager, G. B. Ollivant Ltd . (1961)All

N.L.R. 116; Martins v. Federal Administrator

General and Anor   (1963) L. L. R. 65. I also agree

with the judgment of the Court of Appeal, that the

effective Defendant, against whom any claim is

made in the action is the Nigerian Bar Association.

It is obvious from the Statement of Claim of tile

plaintiff, that he has no claim against the General

Council of the Bar, the 2nd Defendant in the action.

It follows therefore that since the only effective

Defendant is not a juristic person there is no

Defendant before the court to answer the

declarations sought. In  Okechukwu and Sons v.

Ndah  (1967) N. M. L. R. 369 at p. 370, late Idigbe,

C,J. (as he then was) of Midwestern State stated

the position clearly when he declared;

"There is no doubt that a person who should

commence action in court must be a person known

to the law, i.e. a legal person. If it is successfully

shown that a party to an action is not a legal

person, the party should be struck out of the suit. .."

Following this principle, the Court of Appeal was

right in both striking out the 1st appellant from the

suit and in dismissing the action. The appeal can be

determined on this ground alone. I shall rest my

judgment on these grounds alone whilst I agree

with and adopt opinion expressed on the other

grounds by my learned brother, Agbaje, J.S.C.

For the reasons I have given above, I hereby

dismiss the appeal of the appellant with N500 as

costs to each set of Respondents.

reading in draft the lead judgment of my learned

brother, Agbaje, J .S.C. which had just been

delivered. I am in complete agreement with his

reasoning and his conclusion that the appeal is

devoid of merit and should be dismissed.

The only aspect of this case on which I would like to

made by the learned trial Chief Judge restraining

CHUKWUDIFU AKUNNE OPUTA, J.S.C. : I have

had the privilege of a preview in draft of the

marathon judgment just

delivered by my noble and learned brother, Agbaje,

J.S.C. His examination and treatment of the various

Statutes, Decrees, Acts and subsidiary legislations

mentioned in the long but erudite Brief of the

appellant was rather exhaustive. His consideration

of the various legal issues raised in the equally

brilliant Briefs filed by the Respondents was

comprehensive. That being so, one is naturally

tempted to say "I concur, I have nothing else to

add." But the Personality Conception of legal entity

is so important to procedural law that one is obliged

to make some contribution, no matter how small to

the debate on the issue.

How did it all arise? The Plaintiff now Appellant

sued the Nigerian Bar Association as 1st Defendant

and the General Council of the Bar as 2nd

Defendant by an Originating Summons claiming

two Declarations. After the break-down of

negotiations for reconciliation, spearheaded by no

less a legal giant than Sir Adetokunbo Ademola, the

first indigenous Chief Justice of this country, to

have this dispute concerning our learned and

honorable profession settled in a learned and

honorable way, in the interest of the dignity and

integrity of the profession, irrespective of who was

right and who was wrong; after this, three Senior

Advocates of Nigeria, Chief F.R.A. Williams, S.A.N.,

Mr. E. A. Molajo, S.A.N. and Mr. Kehinde Sofola,

S.A.N., who incidentally were also invited to the

abortive reconciliation exercise, appeared for the

1st Defendant - the Nigerian Bar Association. They

were not parties to the dispute. They merely

appeared as counsel to the Nigerian Bar

Association, and that is why I referred to them in

the title as Respondents only and not as

Defendants/Respondents. Only the 1st and the 5th

I referred to as Defendants/Respondents

respectively. The appearance of the 3 Senior

Advocates for the Nigerian Bar Association seems

to have widened the area of controversy. Pursuant

to that appearance, two motions were filed:

1. One by the plaintiff/appellant brought under the

Inherent Jurisdiction of the Court for "an Order of

the Interlocutory Injunction restraining Chief for R.

A. Williams, S.A.N., Mr. Kehinde Sofola, S.A.N. and

Mr. E. A. Molajo, S.A.N., from acting or from

continuing to act or from representing or from

continuing to represent the Nigerian Bar

Association, the 1st Defendant in this suit on the

ground that their appearance or representation for

the Nigerian Bar Association is improper,

unprofessional, dishonourable and dishonest" (see

p. 147 of the record).

2. The second motion brought by Chief Williams for

the 1st Defendant, was for "an order:

(a) striking out the name of the 1st Defendant on

the ground that it is not a juristic person and so

cannot be sued;

(b) striking out the entire action on the ground that

even if all the facts pleaded in the Statement of

Claim are admitted or established, the Court will

not grant any of the reliefs claimed in the absence

of all the proper parties to the action." (see p. 164

of the record)

In his Ruling on the two motions set

out above, the learned trial Chief Judge of Lagos

State held inter alia:

"1. "That the Nigerian Bar Association, the 1st

Defendant is a juristic person and that it was

properly sued by the applicant as a Defendant in

this suit (see p. 192 lines 25-28).

2. The motion. . . praying the Court to strike out

the entire action is in my considered view

misconceived and is accordingly dismissed (see p.

192 lines 29-32).

3. On the prevailing facts of the present situation

and in exercise therefore of the Court's inherent

Jurisdiction and in spite of the misconceived basis

upon which the applicant has founded his motion

the Court is able and thus therefore modify the

order prayed for, for an interlocutory injunction to

an order of injunction simplicity. The three learned

Senior Advocates of Nigeria, Chief Williams, Mr.

Kehinde Sofola, and Mr. Malojo, are therefore

hereby restrained from further appearance for any

of the parties, in this case as presently

constituted" (see p. 199 lines 26-35 and p. 200

line 1).

The trial Chief Judge thus resolved all the issues

arising in the two motions in favour of the plaintiff.

He also allowed the 3 Senior Advocates to appeal

against his order of injunction made against them.
