appealed against the Ruling of the learned Chief

Judge to the Court of Appeal, Lagos Division, coram

Nnaemeka-Aku, Kutigi and Kolawole, H.C.A. In a

lead judgment by Nnaemeka-Aku (J.C.A. as he then

was), to which Kutigi and Kolawole, H.C.A.

concurred, the Court of Appeal held (beautifully

summarised by Kolawole, J.C.A. at p. 424) that:

"(1) The N.B.A. is not a juristic person capable of

being sued in its name. (2) The plaintiff has waived

all objections which could have taken to the

appearance of the three Senior Advocates of

Nigeria.

(3) The evidence of what took place at the

residence of Sir Adetokunbo Ademola was

inadmissable at the hearing of the plaintiff's

application.

(4) The learned Chief Judge was in error in

expressing the opinion that the three Senior

Advocates had "breached their duties to the

administration of Justice."

(5) There was absoluely no ground for

making an order for injunction against the three

Senior advocates."

The appeals of the 1st Defendant, the Nigerian

Bar Association and of the three Senior Advocates

thus succeeded in their entirety.

It definitely does look like legal quibbling to hold in

one breath that the Nigerian Bar Association is not

a juristic person, not a legal persona, and in

another breath to sanction that that non-existent

legal entity can be represented by counsel and can

successfully prosecute an appeal. And therein lies

the complexities of the legal personality concept.

No one is doubting that the Nigerian Bar

Association is not an entity. It is definitely a

collection of all the legal practitioners compelled by

law to become its members. Chief Gani Fawehinmi

thus referred to the Nigerian Bar Association as an

"involuntary association" of lawyers. Chief Williams

in his Brief put the issue correctly thus:

"The issue is simply whether or not the N.B.A. has

capacity to sue or to be sued eo nomine i.e. in its

own name. This is the same thing as the question

whether or not the N.B.A. is a "juristic person" or

whether or not it is a "legal person." It is very

important to emphasise that the case for these

Respondents is not that the N.B.A. cannot sue or be

sued. The Respondent's case is that the N.B.A. can

only sue or be sued by the representative action

procedure prescribed by the Rules of the Court and

never in its own name" . . . By way of illustration,

reference may be made to the portion of the

judgment where the learned Chief Judge referred

to the fact that under Section 7(4)(c) of the Legal

Practitioners Act, 1975 , the N.B.A. is entitled to

receive three quarters of the aggregate amount of

the practising fees collected from all Practitioners

by the registrar. He then posed the question:

"Can one doubt the right of the Association to

institute a claim for the recovery of such sum if it is

not paid over to it by the Registrar?"

The question shows a misconception of the

Respondent's case. It does not reflect the fact that

both parties would answer that question in the

affirmative and that the only dispute between them

is whether the N.B.A. should bring such claim in its

own name (as the plaintiff contends) or by the

representative action procedure prescribed by the

rules of Court (as the Defendants contend)".

It is therefore common ground that the Nigerian

Bar Association can sue and can be sued. The only

dispute is, will it sue eo nomine because it is a legal

persona OR will it sue by a representative action

procedure because it is merely a collection of

individuals with no separate legal existence of its

own?

Now if the Nigerian Bar Association has legal

personality then it can sue eo nomine. If it has no

legal personality then it can only sue by a

representative action for it certainly is a body or an

association consisting of many members (many

human beings).

There is no doubt that a human being is a person in

the eyes of the law - to use the Latin alternative a

"persona." Law in this regard takes account of

human beings so far as their jural relations are

involved. This in Roman law meant the power to

sue as well the power to own property. English law

took over the popular reference of the word

"person" to human beings as its point of reference,

as well as its starting point. It gradually extended

the term "person" to include artificial entities like

corporations. Now what and what are common to a

human being and a corporation? Each is a unit of

jural relations. The concern of the law is to

organise masses of jural relationships whether

centred on an individual or a group. In

jurisprudence therefore a "person" is capable of

having rights and of being liable to duties in

contradistinction to a "thing" which is always the

subject of rights and duties. Now the legal concept

of a human being is simply a multitude of claims,

duties, liberties etc. treated as a unit. If therefore

the law invests an artificial entity like corporation

with a "multitude of claims, duties, liberties, etc." it

likewise invests it with the status of a legal person

or a persona. There is therefore no distinction in

law between a "natural" and "legal person." Both

are legal personae and each is legal persona. The

position then is that legal personality is an artificial

creation of the law. It should be obvious that not all

human beings possess full legal personality. Thus

infants, lunatics and idiots possess but a "restricted

legal personality" hence some sue by their next

friends, others by their guardians.

Since the law is the sole grantor of legal

personality, in any given case, the issue will be -

has the law granted legal personality to the body

under discussion here, the Nigerian Bar

Association? Starting from the known to the

unknown, one quickly finds that in addition to

human beings the law created artificial persons:

(i) The development of trade had enlarged the

grouping of jural relations in such a way as to

embrace collections of individuals organised in what

is known as a corporation aggregate. Incorporated

bodies like companies are thus persons under the

law. The Nigerian Bar Association is definitely not a

company.

(ii) The Corporation sole like the Bishop of a

diocese with perpetual succession has been

invested with legal personality by the law. The

Nigerian Bar Association is not a Corporation Sole.

(iii) Certain unincorporated associations have been

granted the status of legal person by the law:

(a) Registered trade unions have the power granted

them by the law to bring actions eo nomine:

National Union of General and Municipal Workers v.

Gillian (1946) K.B. 81; (1945) 2 All E.R. 593;

British Motor Trade Association v. Salvadori (1949)

Ch. 556; (1949) 1 All E.R. 208; Taff Vale Rail Co.

v. Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants

(1901) A.C. 426.

In this case, it is not contended that the N.B.A. is a

trade union and I dare say it will be derogatory to

the honour and dignity of the Bar to regard the

N.B.A. as a trade union. A trade union has some of

the essential characteristics of a legal person

including the power to sue and be sued given to it

by law. Thus, in Bonsor v. Musicians' Union (1956)

A.C. 104: (1955) 3 All E.R. 518 the House of Lords

held that a member can sue a trade union as a

legal entity for breach of contract.

(b) Partnerships - By the Partnership Act 1890 S.

24(2) a firm can sue and be sued in its own name.

The Nigerian Bar Association is not a partnership.

(c) Friendly Societies - There are special statutory

provisions by which these societies can sue and be

sued in their registered names. Now a friendly

society is a voluntary association formed for the

purpose of raising, by subscription of members,

funds out of which advances may be made for the

mutual relief and the maintenance of the members

and their families in sickness, infancy, old age or

infirmity. The N.B.A. is definitely not a friendly

society inspite of that fraternity for which the Bar is

noted. Also as Chief Gani Fawehinmi himself

pointed out the N.B.A. far from being a voluntary

association is an "involuntary association" for by

Section 2 of the Legal Practitioners Act, 1975 ,

membership is not optional, it is not voluntary, it is

imperative and involuntary.

Having above surveyed the principal and usual

jural units to which the law ascribes legal

personality namely:

(i) Human beings;

(ii) Companies incorporated under the various

Companies Acts;

(iii) Corporation sole with perpetual succession;

(iv) Trade Unions;

(v) Partnerships; and

(vi) Friendly societies;

and having found that the N.B .A. cannot easily be

fitted into any of the above jural units, one then

starts to wonder the quo warranto by which the

N.B.A. was constituted a jural unit and invested by

law with legal personality.

Our problem is to find which law, if any, created

the N.B.A., conferred on it rights and duties, and

prescribed penalties for breaches of those rights

and duties. All these form the contents of those

jural relationships which will inevitably lead to the

inference that legal personality has been conferred

on a jural unit. Because of the necessities and

exigencies of modern commerce and business, the

law wisely treated corporations, trade unions,

partnership etc. as legal persons. "If the law allows

men to form permanently organised groups" wrote

Maitland (in his Collected Papers 111, 314) "those

groups will be for common opinion, right and duty

bearing units; and if the law giver will not openly

treat them as such he will misrepresent or as the

French say, he will 'denature' the facts; in other

words, he will make a mess and call it law." In this

particular case, has the law allowed lawyers to form

the Nigerian Bar Association as a permanently

organised association of lawyers? The answer here

seems to be yes. Then we come to stage 2. Is the

association, the Nigerian Bar Association, a right

and duty bearing unit? That is the crux of the

matter. Chief Gani Fawehinmi has studiously and

meticulously set out nearly all the laws ever

enacted relating to the N.B.A. One has now to

examine those laws closely to find out whether

anyone of them or a combination of some of them,

conferred rights and imposed duties on the N.B.A.

in relation with the plaintiff such that unless legal

personality is ascribed to the N.B.A. an injustice to

the plaintiff/appellant might result: Thomas v. Local

Government Service Board (1965) 1 All N.L.R. 168

pp. 171/172 refers. Both sides relied on Thomas v.

Local Government Service Board supra and I am

glad they did because that case is crucial to a right

determination of the central issue in this appeal.

However, Patton in his Jurisprudence 2nd ed. pp.

334/335 warned:

"But it can hardly be claimed that legal personality

should be automatically achieved as soon as a

group develops a certain stage of organisation - if

only for convenience, the law demands compliance

with certain formalities as a condition of the grant

of legal personality."

This has to be so because legal personality as a

legal concept pre-supposes the corpus - here the

N.B .A. - into which the law infuses the animus of a

fictitious personality. Legal personality is not

reached until the law recognises, over and above

the associated individuals a single entity which in a

manner represents them, but is not identical with

them. As I observed earlier on legal persons are

arbitary creations of the law.

What law credited the N.B.A.? Chief Fawehinmi

referred to the Constitution, Standing Orders, and

Bye Laws of the Nigerian Bar Association copied at

pp. 17 to 42. Without taking isue on whether that

Constitution is or is not a subsidiary legislation, it is

my humble view that a body has, first of all, to

come into existence before it can talk of having a

constitution, standing orders and bye laws. These

are or should be extrinsic to the body itself. These -

constitution, standing orders, bye laws - prove that

the N.B.A. has developed an appreciable stage of

organisation. Now what law created the N.B.A.

before it was able to give itself a constitution? That

is the question. Statutory creation of a jural unit

into a legal persona should be an act easily

referable to one particular statute, for once a unit

is thus created a legal persona it acquires that

status and retains it until the law says or acts

otherwise. I therefore agree with the remarks in

the opinion expressed by the St. Louis Court of

Appeal in Forest City Manufacturing Co. & Ors. v.

Garment Workers Union 223 M.a. App. 935 at p.

943 cited by Nnaemeka-Agu, J .C.A. (as he then

was) at p. 394 of the record that:

"It is inconceivable to think that one desiring to

learn if a particular association has been

constituted a suable entity should be put to the

task of leafing meticulously through the pages of

the statutes and subsequent session acts to see per

chance if that association had somewhere and

sometime been accorded a privilege of any

character not accorded to individuals or

partnerships and it is equally inconceivable to think

that the Legislature, if it had ever desired to

constitute a voluntary unincorporated association a

suable entity, would have done so by the strained

and indirect method contended by the Respondent,

that is, by exempting it from the income tax laws,

or by giving it the right to select a union label,

determine where the same should be displayed, or

by giving it the right to be represented by a

member on the State Board of Mediation."

In other words not all privileges granted to an

association unincorporated will lead to an inference

that legal personality was thus being granted.

There must exist generally a right and duty

relationship before legal personality will be implied.

The court is grateful to Chief Williams for making

available to it Photostat copies of the full report to

the Forest City Manufacturing Co's case .

It does not take more than one stature, in fact one

Section of the Statute, to invest legal personality

on an unincorporated association. If it is not

possible to find that solitary statute, then the

inevitable inference is that the association has not

been granted juristic personality by the law. Thus

Section 1 of the Legal Practitioners Decree (now

Act) 1975 in clear unambiguous language created

an artificial unit called the General Council of the

Bar - the 5th Defendant/Respondent in this case.

The same cannot be said of the Nigerian Bar

Association. Tracing all the Statutes from 1933 to

1979, which recognised the N.B.A, is to my mind

begging the question. The issue is which particular

Statute created the N.B.A. a legal persona? Which

statute made the N.B.A. a suable entity? Which

statute created the N.B.A. a jural unit with rights

and duties relationship generally or at least with

the plaintiff/appellant which will compel the Courts

in the interest of justice to hold that injustice will

occur to the plaintiff/appellant unless the

association is held to be suable eo nomine? These

are the relevant questions pleading for appropriate

answers. The argument that the N.B.A. is

recognised by many statutes, Acts or enactments is

not the answer for the word "recognise" is not

univocal, that is, specifically referable to a

recognition of its juristic personality. On the

contrary, it is equivocal and may properly be

referable to any of the many aspects of the

organisation. For instance, what was it in the

N.B.A. that these enactments recognised - is it the

name N.B.A. or the fact that there is an association

of lawyers known as and called the Nigerian Bar

Association. For that body to acquire the status of

"an artificial person" known to the law, it has either

to be incorporated, or the self same law will clearly

and unequivocally invest it with juristic personality.

No enactment cited by Chief Gani Fawehinmi has

gone that far.

It is true that Section 7(4)(c) of the Legal

Practitioners Decree No. 15 of 1975 imposed an

obligation on the Registrar to pay over to the

N.B.A. 9/10 of the aggregate amount of practising

fees received by him from lawyers, and that the

N.B.A. should keep audited account of all such

monies received. It is also true that the N.B.A. is

required by Section 9(2)(c) of Act No. 15 of 1975 to

nominate twelve practitioners to the Legal

Practitioners Disciplinary Committee. The N.B.A.

also nominates some of its members to the Body of

Benchers. All these are conceded. But these are not

the type of jural relationships required to lead to an

irresistible conclusion that the law intended to

create or constitute the N.B.A. into a juristic

person. But why should one go through this

circuitous route whereas the law, if it wanted, could

simply have said "There shall be created a

constituted body known as the N.B.A." It is as

simple as that. The inevitable conclusion that one is

forced to arrive at is that the N.B.A. is an

unincorporated body of persons. Such a body is not

bereft of rights and remedies. The problem of how

to adapt legal proceedings to unincorporated

societies or associations consisting of many

members is by no means new. These have to

proceed by a representative action procedure. Chief

Williams admits and concedes this much. In other

words, the Plaintiff/Appellant can still press his

claim but by a representative action procedure. My

answer to the question:

"Whether the Nigerian Bar Association is a juristic

person capable of suing and being sued in its

name?"

Is No. It is not. Being an unincorporated

association, it has to sue or be sued by and in a

representative action procedure. It has the corpus -

the de facto association - but the law has not

infused into the corpus the animus of legal

personality. It is a juridical entity but it has not yet

acquired a juristic personality.

I will now review some of the decided cases cited to

show that the N.B.A. although unincorporated

should be regarded as having been impliedly

granted a legal personality. Both sides cited and

relied on Chief Andrew Thomas v. Local

Government Service Board (1965) 1 All N.L.R. 168.

In this case, the Board was sued. It was the

contention of the Board that it was not a suable

entity. The Local Government Service Board was

created and established (not just recognised) by

the Local Government Law of the Western Region

of Nigeria. The Board has to discharge certain

functions under the law. The law creating the Board

made no provisions regarding whether it may sue

or be sued or whether it could own property. I dare

say these are some of the indicia of legal

personality. This Court in the peculiar

circumstances of Thomas' case including the fact

that the Board was created by statute for the

discharge of particular public functions held at pp.

171/172:

"We reject the submission that a statutory body

with functions like those of the Local Government

Service is not liable to be sued for a declaration

and we do so more readily since the statutory

provisions relating to the appellant's office are such

that injustice might result if the Board could not be

made a Defendant to any kind of proceedings. . . so

far as the Board is concerned we are of the opinion

that the Customary Court Law impliedly confers on

it the right to be a party to an action for

declaration. . ." (the italics are mine).

It is clear in Thomas' case above that it was the

Court itself, in the exercise of its interpretative

jurisdiction, that ascribed to the Board some of the

elements of legal personality namely the power to

sue or be sued. This sums to confirm the dicta in

Bonsor v. Musicians' Union (1956) A.C. 104 at pp.

144 & 157 that the categories of legal personae are

not closed. More and more entities will definitely be

brought in, at least, by the Courts, if the justice of

the case so dictates. The question now arises - Is

the present case on all fours with Thomas' case

supra?

The learned trial Chief Judge at p. 186 lines 26-35

and p. 187 lines 1 and 2 of the record reproduced

the same portion of the Supreme Court's judgment

in Thomas' case supra that I set out above. Chief

Gani Fawehinmi in his Brief dealt with the same

case at pp. 17 to 19 and also reproduced that very

same portion of the judgment in Thomas v. Local

Government Board supra. But with respect, the

learned Chief Judge and Chief Gani Fawehinmi did

not draw the necessary distinction between the

case now on appeal and Thomas' case namely:

(i) In Thomas' case the Local Government Board

was created by Statute the Customary Court Law.

In the case on appeal no particular Statute has

been identified as the one that created the N .B.A.

All the available submission is that many

enactments recognised the existence of the N.B.A.

(ii) The Board in Thomas' case had and was charged

with the discharge of public functions. That the

N.B.A. collects a percentage of practising fees from

the Registrar and appoints or nominates members

to the Disciplinary Committee or to the Body of

Benchers, I will regard as "private domestic

function" relating only to the legal profession.

These do not affect the public at large.

(iii) This Court was forced to the conclusion (in

Thomas' case) quoted by the learned Chief Judge

and by Chief Gani Fawehinmi because the statutory

provisions and obligations imposed on the Board

related to "the appellant's office." There was thus a

nexus between the statutory functions of the Board

and the injury complained of by the appellant in

that case. I can see no such nexus between the

duty to collect 9/10 of practising fees from the

registrar, the right or privilege to nominate

members to the Disciplinary Committee and to the

Body of Benchers and the Declarations sought by

the Plaintiff/Appellant in this case.

The facts of Thomas' case and the case now on

appeal are different. And it is the facts of any

particular case that will frame the issues for

decision. The portion of the judgment in Thomas'

case supra which I reproduced above (and which

the trial Chief Judge and Chief Gani Fawehinmi

relied upon) cannot without violence to the facts of

the present case be comfortably applied to this

case. To do so will be to misapply the principle of

the decision in Thomas v. Local Government Board

supra - or to apply the principle out of its proper

context.

The next case relied upon by Chief Gani Fawehinmi

was William kpebimoh v. The Board of Governors

Western Ijaw Teachers' Training College (1966) 1

N.M.L.R. 130. This is a High Court decision. All the

same, it expresses beautifully the point made by

this Court in Thomas v. Local Government Board

supra. In fact the presiding Judge, Arthur Prest, J.

relied on Thomas' case supra and on the House of

Lords' decision in Taff Vale Rail Co. v. Amalgamated

Society of Railway Servants (1901) A.C. 426. Again

the facts of Kpebimoh's case supra that led to the

decision quoted by Chief Gani Fawehinmi at p. 19

of his Brief were that:

(i) The Board was a creature of Statute - the

Education Law of Western Nigeria (applicable to

Mid-Western Nigeria).

(ii) The Board has statutory functions the

management of educational institutions.

(iii) The law establishing the Board did not

specifically give it the right to sue or be sued.

(iv) The plaintiff complained of the breach of his

contract with the Board

by the Board. .

In the above circumstances, Arthur Prest,

J. held, rightly in my view, that:

(i) An unincorporated body which is empowered by

the Legislature to do certain things which can result

in injury to others must be taken to have impliedly

the power to sue or be sued.

(ii) Having regard to the statutory functions of the

Defendant/Board, though it is not an incorporated

body, it is capable of being sued as a legal entity

distinct from its members.

The ratio decidendi of the above case quoted in p.

19 of Chief Gani Fawehinmi's Brief will apply to the

case now on appeal if and only if the facts of the

two cases are the same or similar. But they are

not. The N.B.A. was not created by any Stature.

The functions it has (even if they can be called

statutory) namely to receive a percentage of

practising fees from the registrar, to nominate

members to the Disciplinary Committee and to the

Body of Benchers are not the subject of the present

controversy. Any injury the plaintiff/appellant

alleges he suffered was not inflicted by the N.B.A.

in exercise of any of its statutory functions above

mentioned. That seems to be the rationale of the

decision in Thomas and Kpebimoh supra.

It is good to call the Court's attention to its

pronouncements in a previous case. Under our

system (which we inherited from England and from

the common law) the formulation of general

principles has not preceded decisions. Our case law

is the law of the practitioner rather than the law of

the philosopher. Decisions have drawn their

inspiration and their strength from the very facts

which framed the issues for decision. Once made,

these decisions control future judgments of the

Courts in like or similar cases. The facts of two

cases must be either the same or at least similar

before the decision in one can be used and even

there as a guide to the decision in another case.

What the former decision establishes is only a

principle not a rule. Rules operate in an all or

nothing dimension. Principles do not. They merely

form a principium, a starting point. Where one

ultimately lands will then depend on the peculiar

facts and circumstances of the case in hand. I will

say the same for all the other cases cited in the

appellant's Brief.

It is clear from the declarations claimed that the

real Defendant in this case was the Nigerian Bar

Association. Nothing has really been claimed

against the General Council of the Bar. If the real

substantial Defendant, the N.B.A., is struck out as

not being a suable legal entity, that will be the end

of the proceedings. The Court of Appeal was

therefore right in dismissing the Plaintiff/Appellant's

action in limine.

In the final result and for the reasons given above

and for the fuller reasons in the lead judgment of

my learned brother, Agbaje, J.S.C., which I now

adopt as mine, I, too, will dismiss this appeal. I will

abide by all the consequential orders in the lead

judgment.
